ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The distance between two smooth parallel metal rails is $L=0.4\mathrm{m}$, and the plane of the metal rails is inclined at an angle $\theta=37^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. Within the plane of the rails, there is a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of the rails. A conductor rod ab with mass $m=0.04\mathrm{kg}$ is placed perpendicularly on the metal rails. When the power is turned on and a constant current $I=1.5\mathrm{A}$ flows through the rails, the conductor rod remains stationary. The acceleration due to gravity is taken as $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2$. It is known that $\sin37^{\circ}=0.6$ and $\cos37^{\circ}=0.8$.

1. What is the magnitude of the magnetic induction of the magnetic field?
2. If the direction of the magnetic field is suddenly changed to vertically upward while keeping all other conditions unchanged, what is the acceleration of the conductor rod at the instant after the direction of the magnetic field is changed?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there are two smooth parallel metal guide rails, and the plane in which the guide rails lie is inclined relative to the horizontal plane, with an inclination angle θ marked beside it. The conductor rod ab spans across the two guide rails and is perpendicular to the guide rails. The figure also marks symbols related to the direction of the magnetic field; the initial situation corresponds to the magnetic field being perpendicular to the plane in which the guide rails lie. Reasoning: The guide rails are smooth, so there is no friction force along the direction of the guide rails. Initially the conductor rod is stationary, and the forces are balanced along the direction of the inclined plane. The component of gravity downward along the guide rails is mg sinθ; the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the guide rails, and the magnitude of the Ampere force on the current-carrying rod is F=BIL, with the direction upward along the guide rails to balance the component of gravity. Therefore BIL=mg sinθ. Substituting m=0.04 kg, g=10 m/s², sin37°=0.6, I=1.5 A, L=0.4 m: B=mg sinθ/(IL)=(0.04×10×0.6)/(1.5×0.4)=0.24/0.6=0.4 T. After the magnetic field is suddenly changed to vertically upward, the magnitude of the magnetic induction is still B=0.4 T, and the other conditions remain unchanged. The conductor rod is placed transversely, and the magnitude of the Ampere force it receives is still BIL=0.4×1.5×0.4=0.24 N; judging according to the direction of the current shown in the figure and the direction corresponding to the equilibrium situation given in the problem, this force is a horizontal force, and its component upward along the inclined plane is BIL cosθ=0.24×0.8=0.192 N. The component of gravity downward along the inclined plane is still mg sinθ=0.24 N. Therefore the resultant force along the direction of the inclined plane is mg sinθ−BIL cosθ=0.24−0.192=0.048 N, directed downward along the inclined plane. The acceleration a=F_net/m=0.048/0.04=1.2 m/s², directed downward along the inclined plane.
